Partite saturation number of cycles

Yiduo Xu ††thanks: E-mail:xyd23@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China    Zhen He ††thanks: Corresponding author. E-mail:zhenhe@bjtu.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Beijing Jiaotong University, Beijing 100044, China.    Mei Lu ††thanks: E-mail:lumei@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
Abstract

A graph HH is said to be FF-saturated relative to GG, if HH does not contain any copy of FF, but the addition of any edge ee in E⁡(G)\E⁡(H)E(G)\backslash E(H) would create a copy of FF. The minimum size of an FF-saturated graph relative to GG is denoted by s​a​t​(G,F)sat(G,F). Let KknK_{k}^{n} be the complete kk-partite graph containing nn vertices in each part and CℓC_{\ell} be the cycle of length ℓ\ell. In this paper we give an asymptotically tight bound of s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) for all ℓ≥4,k≥2\ell\geq 4,k\geq 2 except (ℓ,k)=(4,4)(\ell,k)=(4,4). Moreover, we determined the exact value of s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) for k>ℓ=4k>\ell=4 and 5≥ℓ>k≥35\geq\ell>k\geq 3 and (ℓ,k)=(6,2)(\ell,k)=(6,2).

Keywords. saturation number, saturation graph, partite graph, cycle

1 Introduction

In this paper we only consider finite, simple and undirected graphs. For a graph GG, we use V⁡(G)V(G) to denote the vertex set of GG, E⁡(G)E(G) the edge set of GG, |G||G| the order of GG and e⁡(G)e(G) the size of GG. For a positive integer kk, let [k]:={1,2,…,k}[k]:=\{1,2,\ldots,k\}. We say a graph GG is a kk-partite graph, if V⁡(G)V(G) can be partition into kk parts V1,…,VkV_{1},\ldots,V_{k} such that each of ViV_{i} is an independent set. For a kk-partite graph GG, we simply write G=V1∪V2∪⋯∪VkG=V_{1}\cup V_{2}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k}, where ViV_{i} is the ii-th part of GG. Still we abbreviate GG as bipartite if k=2k=2, tripartite if k=3k=3 and multipartite if k≥3k\geq 3. Denote by Cr,PrC_{r},P_{r} the rr-vertices cycle and path, respectively. The length of a path (cycle) is the vertex number of the path (cycle).

For a graph GG and e∉E⁡(G)e\not\in E(G), we use G+eG+e to denote the graph obtained by adding the edge ee into GG. Similarly, given a graph GG and u∈V⁡(G),e∈E⁡(G)u\in V(G),e\in E(G), let G−uG-u (resp. G−eG-e) be the graph obtained by deleting the vertex uu and all edges relating to uu (resp. deleting the edge ee) in GG. For a vertex set (resp. an edge set) AA, let G⁡[A]G[A] be the subgraph of GG induced by AA.

For a graph GG and u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G), let NG​(u)={v:u​v∈E⁡(G)}N_{G}(u)=\{v:uv\in E(G)\} be the neighbourhood of uu, and dG​(u)=|NG​(u)|d_{G}(u)=|N_{G}(u)| the degree of uu. We use δ⁡(G)\delta(G) to denote the minimum degree of GG. Without confusion, we abbreviate as N⁡(u)N(u), d⁡(u)d(u) and δ\delta, respectively. For a vertex set AA, let N⁡(A)=⋃u∈AN⁡(u)∖AN(A)=\bigcup\limits_{u\in A}N(u)\,\setminus\,A. Let N⁡[u]=N⁡(u)∪{u}N[u]=N(u)\cup\{u\} and N⁡[A]=N⁡(A)∪AN[A]=N(A)\cup A. If GG is a partite graph, let Ni​(u)=N⁡(u)∩ViN_{i}(u)=N(u)\cap V_{i} and Ni​(A)=N⁡(A)∩ViN_{i}(A)=N(A)\cap V_{i}. The distance d⁡(u,v)d(u,v) between two vertices u,vu,v is the number of edges contained in the shortest path connecting uu and vv. If u,vu,v are not in the same connected components, then d⁡(u,v)=∞d(u,v)=\infty. Let d⁡(u,v)=0d(u,v)=0 if u=vu=v. For a given partite graph GG, we say a nonedge u​vuv is admissible if u,vu,v lie in different parts of GG. We use d​i​a​mp​(G)diam_{p}(G) to denote the maximum distance between two vertices not lie in the same part of GG.

Given graphs GG and FF, we say a subgraph HH of GG is FF-saturated relative to GG, if HH does not contain any copy of FF but the addition of any edge ee in E⁡(G)\E⁡(H)E(G)\backslash E(H) would create a copy of FF. The saturation number of FF relative to GG is denoted by

s​a​t​(G,F)=min⁡{e⁡(H):H​is​F​-saturated relative to ​G}.sat(G,F)=\min\{e(H):H\;\text{is}\;F\text{-saturated relative to }G\}\,.

Let S​a​t​(G,F)={H:H​is​F​-saturated relative to ​G​ and ​e​(H)=s​a​t​(G,F)}Sat(G,F)=\{H:H\;\text{is}\;F\text{-saturated relative to }G\text{ and }e(H)=sat(G,F)\}. If G=KnG=K_{n}, we abbreviate s​a​t​(G,F)sat(G,F) as s​a​t​(n,F)sat(n,F). The first saturation problem was studied in 1964 by Erdős, Hajnal and Moon [7] who proved that s​a​t​(n,Kr)=(r−2)​(n−1)−(r−2)​(r−1)2sat(n,K_{r})=(r-2)(n-1)-\frac{(r-2)(r-1)}{2}. For readers interested in saturation problem, we refer to the survey [5].

Finding cycle saturation number s​a​t​(n,Ck)sat(n,C_{k}) is an interesting problem in extremal graph theory. The saturation number s​a​t​(n,C3)sat(n,C_{3}) is given in [7] mentioned above. Ollmann [19] and Tuza [23] determined s​a​t​(n,C4)=⌊3​n−52⌋sat(n,C_{4})=\lfloor\frac{3n-5}{2}\rfloor for n≥5n\geq 5. Fisher, Fraughnaugh and Langley [9] derived an upper bound of s​a​t​(n,C5)sat(n,C_{5}) and was confirmed to be the exactly value of s​a​t​(n,C5)sat(n,C_{5}) by Chen [3, 4] later, that is s​a​t​(n,C5)=⌈10​(n−1)7⌉sat(n,C_{5})=\lceil\frac{10(n-1)}{7}\rceil for n≥21n\geq 21. Gould, Luczak, Schmitt [14] and Zhang, Luo, Shigeno [25] proved that ⌈7​n6⌉−2≤s​a​t​(n,C6)≤⌊3​n−32⌋\lceil\frac{7n}{6}\rceil-2\leq sat(n,C_{6})\leq\lfloor\frac{3n-3}{2}\rfloor for n≥9n\geq 9. Recently Lan, Shi, Wang and Zhang [17] showed that s​a​t​(n,C6)=43​n+O⁡(1)sat(n,C_{6})=\frac{4}{3}n+O(1) as n≥9n\geq 9. For k≥7k\geq 7, Füredi and Kim [11] showed that (1+1k+2)​n−1≤s​a​t​(n,Ck)≤(1+1k−4)+(k−42)\left(1+\frac{1}{k+2}\right)n-1\leq sat(n,C_{k})\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{k-4}\right)+\binom{k-4}{2} for n≥2​k−5n\geq 2k-5.

Another interesting problem is the partite saturation number, that is to determine s​a​t​(G,F)sat(G,F) for different FF where GG is a partite graph. Let Kn1,n2,…,nkK_{n_{1},n_{2},\ldots,n_{k}} be the complete kk-partite graph containing nin_{i} vertices in the ii-th part. If n1=n2=⋯=nk=nn_{1}=n_{2}=\cdots=n_{k}=n, we abbreviate it as KknK_{k}^{n}. Note that s​a​t​(Kk1,F)=s​a​t​(k,F)sat(K_{k}^{1},F)=sat(k,F), the study of partite saturation number would help us to determine general saturation numbers.

In this paper we focus on the partite saturation number of cycles s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) for all ℓ≥4\ell\geq 4 and k≥2k\geq 2. When k=2k=2 we only consider ℓ\ell being an even integer since there is no odd cycle in a bipartite graph. An easy observation on a cycle-saturated partite graph GG is that GG must be connected. Otherwise, the addition of two vertices from different connected components and different parts of GG would not form a cycle, a contradiction. Hence we have s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)≥k​n−1sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell})\geq kn-1. Moreover, d​i​a​mp​(G)≤ℓ−1diam_{p}(G)\leq\ell-1.

We first focus on bipartite saturation problem. Bollobás [1] and Wessel [24] determined that s​a​t​(K(n,n),K(s,t))=n2−(n−s+1)​(n−t+1)sat(K_{(n,n)},K_{(s,t)})=n^{2}-(n-s+1)(n-t+1), where K(a,b)K_{(a,b)} is the complete bipartite graph with aa vertices in the first part and bb vertices in the second part. Moshkovitz and Shapira [18] conjectured that s​a​t​(Kn,n,Ks,t)≥(s+t−2)​n−⌊(s+t−22)2⌋sat(K_{n,n},K_{s,t})\geq(s+t-2)n-\lfloor(\frac{s+t-2}{2})^{2}\rfloor for sufficiently large nn. This conjectured has been studied by Gan, Korándi, Sudakov [12] and Chakraborti, Chen, Hasabnis [2] separately. The results of [1, 24] showed that s​a​t​(Kn,n,C4)=2​n−1sat(K_{n,n},C_{4})=2n-1. In [6], Dudek and Wojda have asked the problem that determining s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,C2​t)sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2}},C_{2t}) for t>2t>2. We first answer this problem for t=3t=3 and give an upper bound for t≥4t\geq 4.

Theorem 1.1.

For ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3 and n1,n2≥ℓ+2n_{1},n_{2}\geq\ell+2, s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,C2​ℓ)≤n1+n2+ℓ2−3​ℓ+1sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2}},C_{2\ell})\leq n_{1}+n_{2}+\ell^{2}-3\ell+1. Moreover, s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,C6)=n1+n2+1sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2}},C_{6})=n_{1}+n_{2}+1.

For results of saturation in multipartite graph, Sullivan and Wenger [21] gave the bounds of s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,n3,Kℓ,m,p)sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}},K_{\ell,m,p}) for ℓ≥m≥p\ell\geq m\geq p and n1,n2,n3n_{1},n_{2},n_{3} sufficiently large. Moreover, they determined the exact value of s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,n3,Kℓ,ℓ,p)sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}},K_{\ell,\ell,p}) when p=ℓ,ℓ−1p=\ell,\ell-1. He and Lu [15] determined the exact value of s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,n3,t​Kℓ,ℓ,ℓ)sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}},tK_{\ell,\ell,\ell}) for t,ℓ≥1t,\ell\geq 1 and n1,n2,n3n_{1},n_{2},n_{3} sufficiently large. Ferrara, Jacobson, Pfender and Wenger [8] determined s​a​t​(Kkn,K3)sat(K_{k}^{n},K_{3}) for k≥3k\geq 3 and n≥100n\geq 100. Roberts [20] showed that s​a​t​(K4n,K4)=18​n−21sat(K_{4}^{n},K_{4})=18n-21 for sufficiently large nn. Girão, Kittipassorn and Popielarz [13] studied s​a​t​(Kkn,Kr)sat(K_{k}^{n},K_{r}) for k≥r≥3k\geq r\geq 3 and sufficiently large nn. Since [8, 13, 21] have proved that s​a​t​(Kkn,C3)=3​(k−1)​n−6sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{3})=3(k-1)n-6 for k≥3k\geq 3 and large nn, we only consider CℓC_{\ell}-saturated kk-partite graph with ℓ≥4\ell\geq 4 and k≥3k\geq 3. We give the general bounds of s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}).

Theorem 1.2.

For any ℓ≥4,k≥3\ell\geq 4,k\geq 3 and n≥ℓkn\geq\frac{\ell}{k}, s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)≥k​nsat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell})\geq kn.

Proof. Since a cycle-saturated multipartite graph must be connected, we have s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)≥k​n−1sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell})\geq kn-1. Let GG be a CℓC_{\ell}-saturated kk-partite graph with e⁡(G)=s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)e(G)=sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}). If e⁡(G)=k​n−1e(G)=kn-1, then GG is a tree. If there exists u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) such that uu has two neighbours v,wv,w lie in different parts, then G+v​wG+vw does not contain CℓC_{\ell} as a subgraph. Thus the neighbours of any vertex u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) must lie in the same part which shows that GG is bipartite, a contradiction with k≥3k\geq 3. Hence we have e⁡(G)≥k​ne(G)\geq kn. ∎

Theorem 1.3.

For any ℓ>k≥3\ell>k\geq 3, ℓ≥6\ell\geq 6 and n≥⌊ℓ−22⌋n\geq\lfloor\frac{\ell-2}{2}\rfloor,

s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)\displaystyle sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) ≤k​n−ℓ+1+⌊ℓ−22⌋2+2​(ℓ−1−2​⌊ℓ−22⌋)​⌊ℓ−22⌋\displaystyle\leq\;kn-\ell+1+\lfloor\frac{\ell-2}{2}\rfloor^{2}+2\left(\ell-1-2\,\lfloor\frac{\ell-2}{2}\rfloor\right)\lfloor\frac{\ell-2}{2}\rfloor
={k​n+ℓ2−2​ℓ−114,ℓ​ is odd;k​n+ℓ2−4​ℓ4,ℓ​ is even.\displaystyle=\left\{\;\begin{aligned} &kn+\frac{\ell^{2}-2\ell-11}{4}\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is odd}\,;\\ &kn+\frac{\ell^{2}-4\ell}{4}\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is even}\,.\end{aligned}\right.
Theorem 1.4.

For any k≥ℓ≥5k\geq\ell\geq 5 and n≥⌈k+ℓ−22⌉n\geq\lceil\frac{k+\ell-2}{2}\rceil,

s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)\displaystyle sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) ≤k​n+k+ℓ−5+⌊ℓ−42⌋2+2​(ℓ−4−2​⌊ℓ−42⌋)​⌊ℓ−42⌋\displaystyle\leq\;kn+k+\ell-5+\lfloor\frac{\ell-4}{2}\rfloor^{2}+2\left(\ell-4-2\,\lfloor\frac{\ell-4}{2}\rfloor\right)\lfloor\frac{\ell-4}{2}\rfloor
={k​n+k+ℓ2−2​ℓ−154,ℓ​ is odd;k​n+k+ℓ2−4​ℓ−44,ℓ​ is even.\displaystyle=\left\{\;\begin{aligned} &kn+k+\frac{\ell^{2}-2\ell-15}{4}\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is odd}\,;\\ &kn+k+\frac{\ell^{2}-4\ell-4}{4}\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is even}\,.\end{aligned}\right.

Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 give an upper bound of s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) for all ℓ≥4,k≥3\ell\geq 4,k\geq 3 except for ℓ=4\ell=4 and ℓ=5,3≤k≤4\ell=5,3\leq k\leq 4. The three results below show the exact value of s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) under cases 5≥ℓ>k≥35\geq\ell>k\geq 3. In [21] the authors gave an easy proof on s​a​t​(K3n,C4)sat(K_{3}^{n},C_{4}). In this paper we give a different structural proof of s​a​t​(K3n,C4)sat(K_{3}^{n},C_{4}), not only show the exact value of it but also show that the extremal graph of s​a​t​(K3n,C4)sat(K_{3}^{n},C_{4}) is in Ω(4,3,n)\Omega^{(4,3,n)}, where Ω(4,3,n)\Omega^{(4,3,n)} would be defined in Section 3.

Theorem 1.5.

For any n≥2n\geq 2,

s​a​t​(K3n,C4)=3​n,S​a​t​(K3n,C4)=Ω(4,3,n).sat(K_{3}^{n},C_{4})=3n\,,\quad Sat(K_{3}^{n},C_{4})=\Omega^{(4,3,n)}.
Theorem 1.6.

sat(K3n,C5)={ 6,n=2, 3​n+1,n≥3.sat(K_{3}^{n},C_{5})=\left\{\begin{matrix}\;6\,,\quad\quad\;&\quad n=2\,,\\ \;3n+1\,,&\quad n\geq 3\,.\end{matrix}\right.

Theorem 1.7.

For any n≥10n\geq 10, s​a​t​(K4n,C5)=4​n+2sat(K_{4}^{n},C_{5})=4n+2.

Theorem 1.5 shows that the bounds in Theorem 1.2 are tight when ℓ=4,k=3\ell=4,k=3. Theorems 1.1 - 1.7 immediately give Corollary 1.8.

Corollary 1.8.

For any fixed ℓ≥5,k≥3\ell\geq 5,k\geq 3 or ℓ=4,k=3\ell=4,k=3 or even ℓ≥6,k=2\ell\geq 6,k=2,

s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)=k​n+O⁡(k+ℓ2),sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell})=kn+O(k+\ell^{2})\,,

as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty.

For the rest case k≥ℓ=4k\geq\ell=4, we have following results on C4C_{4}-saturated kk-partite graph. When n=1n=1, such value is equal to s​a​t​(k,C4)=⌊3​k−52⌋sat(k,C_{4})=\lfloor\frac{3k-5}{2}\rfloor, answering that studying partite saturation number is useful to determine original saturation number.

Theorem 1.9.

For any k≥5k\geq 5 and n≥1n\geq 1,

sat(Kkn,C4)=⌊3​(k−1)​n−22⌋={32​(k−1)​n−32,k​ is even,n​ is odd;32​(k−1)​n−1,otherwise.sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{4})\;=\;\lfloor\frac{3(k-1)n-2}{2}\rfloor=\left\{\;\begin{aligned} &\frac{3}{2}(k-1)n-\frac{3}{2}\,,&\;&k\text{ is even}\,,\,n\text{ is odd}\,;\\ \\ &\frac{3}{2}(k-1)n-1\,,&\;&\text{otherwise}\,.\\ \end{aligned}\right.

Moreover, ⌊92​n−1⌋≤s​a​t​(K4n,C4)≤5​n−1\lfloor\frac{9}{2}n-1\rfloor\leq sat(K_{4}^{n},C_{4})\leq 5n-1.

For k≥3k\geq 3 and ℓ\ell is much greater than kk, we give a better construction in order to prove that s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)=k​n+O⁡(ℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell})=kn+O(\ell).

Theorem 1.10.

For any fixed k≥4k\geq 4, ℓ≥60​k+12\ell\geq 60k+12 and nn sufficeintly large,

s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)≤k⁡(n−1)+6​⌈ℓ5⌉.sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell})\leq k(n-1)+6\,\lceil\,\frac{\ell}{5}\,\rceil\,.

Moreover, s​a​t​(K3n,Cℓ)≤3​n+13​⌈ℓ5⌉sat(K_{3}^{n},C_{\ell})\leq 3n+13\,\lceil\,\frac{\ell}{5}\,\rceil while n,ℓn,\ell satisfy the same condition.

The existence of limn→∞s​a​t​(n,F)n\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{sat(n,F)}{n} is the most important problem in saturation number. Tuza [22] proved that s​a​t​(n,F)=O⁡(n)sat(n,F)=O(n) for all FF and has conjectured that there exists a constant c=c⁡(F)c=c(F) such that s​a​t​(n,F)=c​n+o⁡(n)sat(n,F)=cn+o(n). This conjectured has been confirmed to be correct for many specific graphs, readers can see them in [5]. Such a conjecture can be asked to partite saturation version.

Conjecture 1.11.

For any fixed k≥2k\geq 2 and FF being a subgraph of KknK_{k}^{n}, limn→∞s​a​t​(Kkn,F)k​n\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{sat(K_{k}^{n},F)}{kn} exists.

The partite saturation results introduced above and all Theorems given in this paper have confirmed that this conjecture is correct for specific graphs. Combining results of [1, 8, 13, 21, 24] we have following Corollary.

Corollary 1.12.

For any fixed ℓ,k≥3\ell,k\geq 3 and even ℓ≥4,k=2\ell\geq 4,k=2 except for (ℓ,k)=(4,4)(\ell,k)=(4,4), limn→∞s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)k​n\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell})}{kn} exists.

From the table below, readers can visualize all Theorems and Corollaries in this section. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we prove Theorem 1.1. In Section 3 we construct saturated subgraphs of KknK_{k}^{n}. We also prove Theorems 1.3, 1.4 and 1.10 in this Section. In Section 4, we prove Theorems 1.5 and 1.9. In Section 5, we prove Theorems 1.6 and 1.7. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section 6 with some open problems.

2 Bipartite saturation number of even cycles

We begin this section by an easy observation, and we would construct C2​ℓC_{2\ell}-saturated bipartite graph for ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3.

Observation 2.1.

For ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3, let H=Kℓ,ℓ−1=V1∪V2H=K_{\ell,\ell-1}=V_{1}\cup V_{2} where |V1|=ℓ,|V2|=ℓ−1|V_{1}|=\ell,|V_{2}|=\ell-1. Then for any different u,v∈V⁡(H)u,v\in V(H),
(1) If u,v∈V1u,v\in V_{1}, then there exists P2​ℓ−1,P2​ℓ−3P_{2\ell-1},P_{2\ell-3} connecting u,vu,v in HH.
(2) If u∈V1,v∈V2u\in V_{1},v\in V_{2}, then there exists P2​ℓ−2P_{2\ell-2} connecting u,vu,v in HH.

Definition 2.2.

Let ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3 and n1,n2≥ℓ+2n_{1},n_{2}\geq\ell+2. Let 𝒢n1,n2ℓ=V1∪V2\mathscr{G}_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{\ell}=V_{1}\cup V_{2} be a bipartite graph such that |V1|=n1,|V2|=n2|V_{1}|=n_{1},|V_{2}|=n_{2}. Let Ai⊆ViA_{i}\subseteq V_{i} be a (ni−ℓ)(n_{i}-\ell)-element vertex set and Bi=Vi∖AiB_{i}=V_{i}\setminus A_{i}. Pick distinct vertices x1,x2∈B1x_{1},x_{2}\in B_{1} and y1∈B2y_{1}\in B_{2}. Then the edge ee in GG can only be :
(1) e=u​y1e=uy_{1} for any u∈A1u\in A_{1} ;
(2) e=v​x1e=vx_{1} for any v∈A2v\in A_{2} ;
(3) e=y1​x2e=y_{1}x_{2} ;
(4) e=x​ye=xy for any u∈B1,v∈B2∖{y1}u\in B_{1},v\in B_{2}\setminus\{y_{1}\}.

Readers can visualize 𝒢n1,n2ℓ\mathscr{G}_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{\ell} in Figure 1. It is clear that e⁡(𝒢n1,n2ℓ)=n1+n2+ℓ2−3​ℓ+1e(\mathscr{G}_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{\ell})=n_{1}+n_{2}+\ell^{2}-3\ell+1.

Proposition 2.3.

𝒢n1,n2ℓ\mathscr{G}_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{\ell} is C2​ℓC_{2\ell}-saturated.

Proof. Obviously all vertices in A1∪A2∪{y1}A_{1}\cup A_{2}\cup\{y_{1}\} are not in cycles, so 𝒢n1,n2ℓ\mathscr{G}_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{\ell} is C2​ℓC_{2\ell}-free. To prove that 𝒢n1,n2ℓ\mathscr{G}_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{\ell} is C2​ℓC_{2\ell}-saturated we only need to show that for any admissible nonedge u​vuv there exists a P2​ℓP_{2\ell} connecting u,vu,v. Let u​vuv be an admissible nonedge. If u∈A1,v∈A2u\in A_{1},v\in A_{2}, by Observation 2.1 there exists P2​ℓ−3P_{2\ell-3} connecting x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} in HH, together with u,v,y1u,v,y_{1} there exists P2​ℓP_{2\ell} connecting u,vu,v. For the rest cases (1) u∈A1,v∈B2′u\in A_{1},v\in B_{2}^{\prime}, (2) u∈B1∖{x1},v∈A2u\in B_{1}\setminus\{x_{1}\},v\in A_{2} and (3) u∈B1∖{x2},v=y2u\in B_{1}\setminus\{x_{2}\},v=y_{2} we are also done by similar arguments using Observation 2.1. Hence 𝒢n1,n2ℓ\mathscr{G}_{n_{1},n_{2}}^{\ell} is C2​ℓC_{2\ell}-saturated. ∎

Proposition 2.4.

For n1,n2≥5n_{1},n_{2}\geq 5, s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,C6)≥n1+n2+1sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2}},C_{6})\geq n_{1}+n_{2}+1.

If r≥5r\geq 5, then the addition of x1​y2x_{1}y_{2} in GG would only create C4C_{4} and cycles of length at least 8, a contradiction. 3 Constructions of saturated subgraphs of KknK_{k}^{n}

In this section, we construct several graph families to show the upper bounds of our saturation results. We begin from a simple proposition.

Proposition 3.1.

Let G=V1∪⋯∪VkG=V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k} be a kk-partite graph. If there exist A⊆V⁡(G)A\subseteq V(G) and x1,…,xk∈Ax_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in A such that:
(1) N⁡(ui)={xi}N(u_{i})=\{x_{i}\} for any ui∈Vi∖Au_{i}\in V_{i}\setminus A and i∈[k]i\in[k], and there exists a Pℓ−1P_{\ell-1} connecting xx and xix_{i} for any x∈A∖(Vi∪{xi})x\in A\setminus(V_{i}\cup\{x_{i}\});
(2) There exists a Pℓ−2P_{\ell-2} connecting xix_{i} and xjx_{j} for any i,j∈[k]i,j\in[k];
(3) G⁡[A]G[A] is CℓC_{\ell}-saturated.
Then GG is CℓC_{\ell}-saturated.

Proof. Obviously, GG is CℓC_{\ell}-free. By (3), we only need to consider an admissible nonedge who has at least one endpoint in V⁡(G)∖AV(G)\setminus A. Let ui​wu_{i}w be an admissible nonedge with ui∈Vi∖Au_{i}\in V_{i}\setminus A, where i∈[k]i\in[k]. If w∈Vj∖Aw\in V_{j}\setminus A for some j∈[k]∖{i}j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}, by (1) and (2), there exists a PℓP_{\ell} connecting uiu_{i} and ww. If w∈Aw\in A, then w∉Viw\notin V_{i}. By (1), there exists a PℓP_{\ell} connecting uiu_{i} and ww. Hence G+ui​wG+u_{i}w would create a CℓC_{\ell} in each case. Thus GG is CℓC_{\ell}-saturated. ∎

Let G=V1∪⋯∪VkG=V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k} be a kk-partite graph and x1,…,xk∈V⁡(G)x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in V(G). We call (x1,…,xk)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) a good pair of GG if they do not lie in the same part of GG.

Lemma 4.8.

Let u,vu,v be the vertices of degree 1 in GG. If u,vu,v lie in different parts of GG, then N⁡(u)≠N⁡(v)N(u)\neq N(v). Moreover, the number of parts containing a degree 1 vertex is at most 3.

Proof. Let u,vu,v be the vertices of degree 1 lie in different parts of GG. If N⁡(u)=N⁡(v)N(u)=N(v), then the addition of u​vuv would only create C3C_{3} in GG, a contradiction.

If there exists xi∈Vix_{i}\in V_{i} such that d⁡(xi)=1d(x_{i})=1 with i∈[4]i\in[4], let N⁡(xi)={yi}N(x_{i})=\{y_{i}\}. Since the addition of xi​xjx_{i}x_{j} would create a C4C_{4}, yi​yj∈E⁡(G)y_{i}y_{j}\in E(G) and hence G⁡[y1,y2,y3,y4]G[y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4}] is a K4K_{4}, a contradiction. ∎

By Lemma 4.8 we know that GG contains at most 3​n3n vertices of degree 1. Moreover, let x1,x2∈Vix_{1},x_{2}\in V_{i} for some ii such that N⁡(x1)={y1},N⁡(x2)={y2}N(x_{1})=\{y_{1}\},N(x_{2})=\{y_{2}\} with y1≠y2y_{1}\neq y_{2}. Then a new graph G′=(G−x2​y2)+x2​y1G^{\prime}=\left(G-x_{2}y_{2}\right)+x_{2}y_{1} is still a C4C_{4}-saturated kk-partite graph with the same number of edges as GG. So we assume that all degree 1 vertices in the same part of GG have the same neighbour.

Proposition 4.9.

If δ⁡(G)=1\delta(G)=1, then e⁡(G)≥⌊3​(k−1)​n−22⌋e(G)\geq\lfloor\frac{3(k-1)n-2}{2}\rfloor.

For a vertex u≠x,yu\neq x,y, let Mi​(u)=N⁡(u)∩SiM_{i}(u)=N(u)\cap S_{i} for i∈[4]i\in[4]. Clearly if u∈Sju\in S_{j} for some jj, then if |i−j|≥2|i-j|\geq 2 we have Mi​(u)=∅M_{i}(u)=\emptyset. Define a weight function ff as :

f(u)={|M1​(u)|+12​|M2​(u)|,u∈S2,|M2​(u)|+12​|M3​(u)|+12​|M4​(u)|,u∈S3,12​|M3​(u)|,u∈S4.f(u)=\left\{\begin{aligned} \;&|M_{1}(u)|+\frac{1}{2}|M_{2}(u)|\,,\;&u\in S_{2}\,,\\ \;&|M_{2}(u)|+\frac{1}{2}|M_{3}(u)|+\frac{1}{2}|M_{4}(u)|\,,\;&u\in S_{3}\,,\\ \ \;&\frac{1}{2}|M_{3}(u)|\,,\;&u\in S_{4}\,.\end{aligned}\right.

Since n≥3n\geq 3, by Lemma 5.5, there exists a B​rjBr_{j} such that r​a​d​(B​rj)=1rad(Br_{j})=1. Assume B​rj={x}Br_{j}=\{x\}, x∈V1x\in V_{1} and x​u2∈E⁡(G)xu_{2}\in E(G). Then G+x​u3G+xu_{3} would not create a C5C_{5}, a contradiction. Hence e⁡(G)≥3​n+1e(G)\geq 3n+1, and we finished the proof of Theorem 1.6. ∎

6 Concluding remark

Determining the value of s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) is an interesting problem in partite saturation number. Although we have determined the value for ℓ>k≥3\ell>k\geq 3 and ℓ=2​r≥6,k=2\ell=2r\geq 6,k=2 asymptotically except for (ℓ,k)=(4,4)(\ell,k)=(4,4), there is still the other half of the problem that needs to be solved urgently. We give our conjectures on such problems.

Problem 6.1.

Determine the value of s​a​t​(Kkn,Cℓ)sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\ell}) for all ℓ≥4,k≥3\ell\geq 4,k\geq 3 and even ℓ≥8,k=2\ell\geq 8,k=2.

Conjecture 6.2.

For ℓ≥4\ell\geq 4 and n1,n2≥ℓ+2n_{1},n_{2}\geq\ell+2, s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,C2​ℓ)=n1+n2+ℓ2−3​ℓ+1sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2}},C_{2\ell})=n_{1}+n_{2}+\ell^{2}-3\ell+1.

Conjecture 6.3.

For n≥1n\geq 1, s​a​t​(K4n,C4)=5​n−1sat(K_{4}^{n},C_{4})=5n-1.

For a given graph family ℱ\mathcal{F}, a graph HH is said to be ℱ\mathcal{F}-saturated in GG if HH does not contain any copy of all graphs in ℱ\mathcal{F}, but the addition of a nonedge in E⁡(G)∖E⁡(H)E(G)\setminus E(H) would form a copy of some F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. Similarly we can define saturation number s​a​t​(G,ℱ)sat(G,\mathcal{F}) and partite saturation number s​a​t​(Kkn,ℱ)sat(K_{k}^{n},\mathcal{F}). Let 𝒞≥ℓ\mathcal{C}_{\geq\ell} be the graph families of cycles with length at least ℓ\ell, i.e. 𝒞≥ℓ={Cℓ,Cℓ+1,…}\mathcal{C}_{\geq\ell}=\{C_{\ell},C_{\ell+1},\ldots\}. Although Theorem 1.10 shows that the Construction I is not optimal, we believe that it is tight when we consider 𝒞≥ℓ\mathcal{C}_{\geq\ell}-saturation. So we have following conjecture.

Conjecture 6.4.

For ℓ>k≥3\ell>k\geq 3, ℓ≥6\ell\geq 6 and sufficiently large nn,

s​a​t​(Kkn,C≥ℓ)=k​n−ℓ+1+⌊ℓ−22⌋2+2​(ℓ−1−2​⌊ℓ−22⌋)​⌊ℓ−22⌋,sat(K_{k}^{n},C_{\geq\ell})\;=\;kn-\ell+1+\lfloor\frac{\ell-2}{2}\rfloor^{2}+2\left(\ell-1-2\,\lfloor\frac{\ell-2}{2}\rfloor\right)\lfloor\frac{\ell-2}{2}\rfloor\,,

and the extremal graphs are all in Ω(ℓ,k,n)\Omega^{(\ell,k,n)}.
